agent_notes: STEPBible glosses אֵל as 'O God of' in both halves and takes נְקָמוֹת as a plural. I keep the plural 'vengeances' in the literal layer, as the Hebrew has it; the English versions all flatten it to 'vengeance'. The vocative אֵל (God) is read as a construct before נְקָמוֹת, with יְהוָה in apposition.
הוֹפִיעַ is glossed 'shine forth' (root יפע). Rashi glosses it 'show and reveal to us your vengeance', Metzudat Zion ties it to Deut 33:2. I follow the light image in both layers.

The second half has no verb of its own in Hebrew ('the teacher of humankind knowledge'). KJV supplies 'shall not he know?' from the sense of v9 and v11; ASV and YLT also supply a clause. I bracket the missing clause in the literal layer and leave it unsupplied in the dramatic layer except as an echo.

history.note: [consider] Attribute the three-item list to Ibn Ezra, and say that Radak names the flood and Sodom. (Radak on PS.94.10: "הביא על הרשעים מי המבול ... וכן אנשי סדום"; Ibn Ezra: "אנשי המבול ודור הפלגה ואנשי סדום")

agent_notes: הֵמָּה refers to the thoughts or to the humans: grammatically it is plural and so matches 'thoughts' (מַחְשְׁבוֹת) better than singular אָדָם, but it could be 'they, the people'. Radak and Metzudat David read the thoughts as futile. I follow the thoughts.

The Hebrew has the divine name in the short form יָהּ (Yah) in vv. 7 and 12. The literal layer keeps 'Yah'; the dramatic layer uses 'the LORD' as the skill asks. The commentary claim that Deut 8:5 and 8:16 stand behind the verse is Radak's and Meiri's own citation, taken from the packet.

Revised after the reviewer's request: the שַׁחַת note no longer claims a shared root with the digging verb. It gives 'pit' (Metzudat Zion: בור), the verb as כרה, and Ibn Ezra's link to השחתה 'destruction'. The five English versions agree on 'pit' except BBE ('a hole ... for the destruction'), which follows the Ibn Ezra line. Rashi, Metzudat David and Meiri read 'the days of evil' as Gehinnom; I translate the Hebrew as it stands and leave the reading to the commentary.
The 'to him' of לוֹ is the man of v12, one who is disciplined and taught. The verse is one sentence with v12 and I kept the syntactic link: 'to give him quiet' is the purpose of the discipline.

agent_notes: עַד־צֶדֶק יָשׁוּב מִשְׁפָּט is difficult: 'to/until righteousness' has no verb of motion before it. I read 'judgment will return to righteousness', following Radak's gloss that justice and righteousness were joined and the wicked separated them. Malbim, Rashi and Metzudat David read it differently, as a statement about suffering or delay. The KJV 'follow it' for the second half is a smoothing: the Hebrew has only 'and after it [will be] all the upright of heart'.

דוּמָה is rendered 'silence' in the literal layer and 'the land of silence' only in the commentary. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri take it as the place of the dead; Rashi and Metzudat Zion point to the plain word 'silence'. The Hebrew keeps both possible, and the English versions split: KJV and YLT keep 'silence', BBE says 'death'.

agent_notes: שַׂרְעַפַּי is rare and I rendered it 'my disquieting thoughts' (the STEPBible gloss); the 'branching' image in the commentary is my own reading of the root and is not sourced. Metzudat Zion links it with Ps 139:23 (שׂרעפי). The verb יְשַׁעַשְׁעוּ is a Pilpel from the root שׁעע: 'to dandle, play with, delight'. Radak and Meiri comment on its unusual vocalization; I do not claim an explanation beyond theirs.

agent_notes: הַוּוֹת: I gloss it 'ruin, disaster' (HALOT, BDB as 'destruction'), against the KJV 'iniquity'. Ibn Ezra calls the verb יְחָבְרְךָ a strange word (מלה זרה); the sense 'be joined to you, be allied with you' is standard. עֲלֵי־חֹק is read 'by decree / under cover of statute'; the preposition could also be 'against'. Rashi's reading of idols is not followed; Radak's of a tyrant's throne, with Nebuchadnezzar named, is a later historical application that I do not adopt as the primary sense.

יָגוֹדּוּ is read as from גדד 'to cut, gash; to band together' (BDB, גּדוּד 'troop'). Rashi, Radak and Metzudat David read it as 'they gather in troops'. Radak and Meiri mention another view, 'they cut / decree' (the Aramaic gadad); Meiri's text has יגורו. KJV 'gather themselves together' follows the troop reading; YLT 'decree' the other. I keep the troop reading and mark the other in the commentary.

וַיְהִי in the packet is glossed 'and he has become'. The verb is a wayyiqtol: 'and he was / became'. A prophetic-perfect or a past after the crisis are both defensible; Meiri reads it as describing the end, Radak and Metzudat David as a past rescue. I give it as a past: 'But the LORD became a refuge for me'. KJV 'But' is the implied contrast, not the Hebrew word.

וַיָּשֶׁב is also a wayyiqtol, and is followed by two imperfects. Radak says a past form stands for a future, 'common in prophetic speech'. I keep the past form in the literal layer and the future-facing 'will' for the imperfects. The doubled יַצְמִיתֵם is kept as repetition, not omitted; the KJV's 'yea' is an addition. The word אוֹנָם is read as 'their wickedness' (from אָוֶן); Rashi and Metzudat Zion link it with 'strength / vigor' (און). The pun between 'Aven (v.16, 'wickedness') and 'onam is not marked in the English versions.

agent_notes: The five English versions split on whether v4 continues the 'how long' of v3 (KJV, Webster) or is a plain statement (YLT, ASV, BBE). The Hebrew has no interrogative, so the literal layer is a plain statement; the dramatic layer lets the tension run on from v3. Malbim's reading (that v4 introduces what the wicked say, in vv. 1-3) is not followed: the sentence reads as the psalmist's description.

יִתְאַמְּרוּ occurs once in the Bible. Rashi and Ibn Ezra tie it to Deut 26:17-18 (הֶאֱמַרְתָּ / הֶאֱמִירְךָ, 'you have declared / made you declare'), giving the sense 'exalt, praise oneself'; STEPBible's 'boast' follows the same lead.

Revised after the reviewer's request: the Radak sentence now says the lawless wicked crush and afflict the strong Israelites, who are protected by the kingdom, and kill the weak, who have no one to demand their blood (Radak on Ps 94:5, with v6). The powerful Israelites are not the oppressors.

agent_notes: יְרַצֵּחוּ is Piel (intensive) of רצח, a verb tied to unlawful killing. Radak raises the possibility of a causative sense ('have others kill them'); I do not adopt it and render 'they murder'.

בֹּעֲרִים is from בער 'to be brutish'; the same root is used of stupid cattle-like behaviour (Ps 73:22). I render 'brutes' in the dramatic layer and 'stupid ones' in the literal layer, which keeps the animal connotation visible.

The verse is a pair of rhetorical questions, each beginning with הֲ. The verbs נָטַע (plant) and יָצַר (form) are participles and are kept as agent nouns ('the planter', 'the former') in the literal layer. This is where the KJV's 'He that planted... shall he not hear?' is faithful; the BBE recasts it.
